Why Siemens’ Breker Deal Matters for the Next Generation of AI Chipsby Daniel Nenni on 11-24-2026 at 8:00 am

View Profile

View Forum Posts

View Articles

Private Message

Categories: Breker Verification Systems, EDA, Siemens EDA

Key takeaways ▼

A chip can pass tests for every major component and still run into trouble when those components work together. A processor, a memory controller and an accelerator can each behave as designed, yet a bug may surface only when all three are busy and software asks the chip to switch power states. That is the kind of problem Siemens is targeting with its agreement to acquire Breker Verification Systems. The deal could give engineers a better way to find those failures while they still have time to fix them.
The timing is promising. AI and high-performance computing are pushing chipmakers toward designs that combine specialized processors, complex memory systems and, increasingly, multiple dies in a single package. At the same time, software has a growing role in how chips manage power, move data and enforce security. Each design choice creates more combinations for verification teams to consider. Even a well-tested design can hide a bug in a sequence of events that nobody thought to test.
Breker’s specialty is automating the creation of those sequences. Its test suite synthesis technology can help engineers turn a verification goal into a set of scenarios they can run and reuse. Imagine an AI accelerator reading from shared memory while a CPU is writing to it and another part of the chip is changing power states. Engineers can use generated scenarios to vary the timing and order of those events, looking for failures that might appear only under a particular combination. Automation gives teams more room to explore those possibilities without having to write every scenario by hand.
That capability fits alongside Siemens’ Questa One verification tools and Avery Verification IP. Protocol verification IP helps engineers check whether an interface follows the rules for exchanging data. Breker brings tools for exercising what happens across several interfaces, components and software workloads in the same test. Used together, these capabilities could help teams build on the work they already do to verify individual components and focus more of their time on what happens when the whole system is running.
The payoff could be especially valuable in AI and high-performance computing, where a problem in how processors and accelerators share memory can be hard to reproduce. The same approach could help automotive chip teams test how a design responds when software requests a power transition while other functions still need to run. And when teams can reuse scenarios across designs, a test written for one project can help a later project catch a similar problem earlier.
The agreement also fits with Siemens’ separately planned acquisition of Lauterbach, which makes tools for debugging embedded systems. The two deals point toward closer coordination between the engineers who verify chips and the developers who write the software that runs on them. When a failure involves both, each team may see only part of what happened. A workflow that lets both teams investigate the same behavior earlier could shorten the time it takes to trace a failure to its source, while design changes are still easier to make.
Siemens expects the Breker transaction to quickly close in December 2026, subject to customary closing conditions. Financial terms were undisclosed. For customers, much will depend on how readily Siemens incorporates Breker’s technology into existing verification workflows. Teams have invested years in their test environments, and the integration will be most useful if engineers can adopt the new capabilities while continuing to use the tests and tools they already rely on.
Bottom line: The reason for optimism is practical. Engineers could spend less time scripting tests one by one and more time investigating the interactions most likely to cause trouble. Finding even one difficult system bug before manufacturing can spare a team an expensive redesign or a delayed launch. If Siemens can make that kind of testing easier to adopt and repeat, the benefit could extend from the first verification run to the products that ultimately ship.
